analysis.one_liner: Lowers federal sugar price supports and raises sugar import quotas to cut consumer sugar prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 48 House members from both parties, never got a vote in either committee that held it and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules keep US sugar prices well above world levels through price supports and import quotas, and consumers and food companies pay the difference. This bill would have cut the government's sugar loan rate by 1.5 cents per pound each year (with a floor of 12 cents), forced sugar import quotas up by 500,000 short tons a year from 1990 through 1993, and narrowed the gap between the official support price and the market price [S2][S3]. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: American households, who pay roughly double the world price for sugar under the quota-and-support system, and food and beverage makers (candy, baked goods, soft drinks) whose sugar costs would fall. Sugar-exporting countries in the Caribbean and elsewhere would regain a share of the US market through the larger quotas [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the federal sugar loan rate 1.5 cents per pound each crop year starting in 1989, with a floor of 12 cents per pound for raw cane sugar, lowering the price floor that keeps domestic sugar expensive

Requires sugar import quotas for 1990-1993 to rise by 500,000 short tons each year (or to whatever level keeps the sugar program operating at no federal cost), increasing supply and pushing consumer prices toward world levels
Directs the Agriculture Secretary to shrink the gap between the loan rate and the market stabilization price and to report to Congress within 90 days on the steps taken

analysis.who_pays: US sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors, who would receive lower prices for their crop as the support floor falls and imports rise, and corn sweetener producers, who would face renewed competition from cheaper sugar in soft drinks and processed foods.

drawbacks.text: Sugar beet and cane farmers and the rural communities that depend on them would see crop prices fall under the bill's mandated yearly 1.5-cent cut in the loan rate
Larger import quotas would shift more of the US sugar supply to foreign producers, which supporters of the existing program argue risks dependence on imports in a disruption
The reform was partial: the bill keeps a 12-cents-per-pound support floor and lets the President set a lower quota if he finds it protects trading partners, so consumer savings would be limited

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades lower incomes for a concentrated domestic sugar industry against lower grocery and food-manufacturing costs for everyone else, and it also protects taxpayers by forcing imports high enough to keep the government from having to buy and store surplus sugar [S3]. The 12-cent floor and the President's discretion to set quotas lower mean the savings would be real but capped [S3]. On balance it is a consumer-oriented reform, though growers in sugar-producing regions would bear the full adjustment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Agriculture and Ways and Means Committees for nearly two years — it got one subcommittee hearing in February 1990 and was never brought up for a vote, dying when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Downey of New York introduced the bill on February 22, 1989, with 17 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture and Ways and Means Committees
It was split between subcommittees — Trade under Ways and Means and Cotton, Rice, and Sugar under Agriculture — in early March 1989

The only action after that was a single subcommittee hearing on February 20, 1990; neither full committee ever reported the bill or brought it to the House floor, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US sugar beet and cane growers and processors, who kept the import quota and price support system that holds US sugar prices well above world levels, and corn sweetener producers, who kept cheaper sugar from competing for their customers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic sugar growers and corn sweetener makers

for.name: Thomas J. Downey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled bipartisan original cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair E. de la Garza)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire Congress, taking only one subcommittee hearing and never reporting it out

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means (Chair Dan Rostenkowski)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Trade Subcommittee, where no further action was ever taken

against.name: US sugar producers
against.role: Industry beneficiaries of the existing sugar program
against.what_they_did: Longstanding defenders of sugar price supports and import quotas, which the bill would have cut

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 27 of 257 House Democrats and 21 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored — but no vote was ever taken, so no party split ever showed up on the record.

industries.industry: US sugar beet and cane growers and processors
industries.note: The bill cuts their price floor by 1.5 cents per pound per year and forces import quotas up by 500,000 tons a year, eroding the protected high domestic price the current program guarantees them. Consumers pay for that protection at the grocery store.

High sugar prices are what make corn sweeteners economical for soft drinks and processed foods; cheaper imported and domestic sugar would take back part of that market. Their interest runs against cheaper sugar for consumers.
Candy, bakery, and soft drink makers buy sugar as a major input, so a lower support price and bigger import quotas directly cut their costs, alongside savings for households.
The quota increase of 500,000 tons a year would restore access to the US market for Caribbean and other developing-country exporters who lost it under the current tight quotas.
